appraisal_events.evidence: « Elle était si bien encagée » ; « cette actrice si convoitée n'était-ce pas elle qui, retirée par moi de la scène, enfermée chez moi, était à l'abri des désirs de tous » ; « je n'étais pas médiocrement fier d'avoir cueilli, dérobé à tous, la plus belle rose » — contre le souvenir d'« une grande actrice de la plage en feu, excitant les jalousies … dominant ses amies ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage measures Albertine's fall from the envied, unapproachable figure who dominated her friends at Balbec to a caged, obedient captive whose empty life supplies only what the narrator demands and whose sleep turns her into a plant. The narrator's proprietary triumph supplies the frame, but the litotes of his pride, the cage vocabulary, and the closing admission « elle me manquait, je ne la possédais pas » undercut the boast rather than endorsing it.

appraisal_events.evidence: « son jugement avait été entièrement renversé. Elle avait découvert chez Morel … des profondeurs de méchanceté et de perfidie … et chez M. de Charlus une insoupçonnable et immense bonté, mêlée de duretés qu'elle ne connaissait pas », après « le rôle de bourreau » et « l'atroce méchanceté du baron ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The reported reversal lifts Charlus from tyrant and torturer to a man of unsuspected immense goodness, while lowering Morel from the violinist of infinite delicacies to one capable of deep malice and perfidy. The narrator immediately relativizes the reversal by ranking it no more definite than his own failed judgments of Andrée and Albertine, so the elevation is reported without being underwritten as knowledge.

status_effects.explanation: She is explicitly sequestered — « encagée », « cloîtrée dans ma maison », « à l'abri des désirs de tous » — cut off from the social space in which she had circulated.

The passage stages her loss of standing directly: once followed by everyone, hard to catch, dominating her friends, she is now defined by the emptiness of her life and by eagerness and obedience toward the narrator.

He gains real leverage — pride at having stolen the finest rose, control over her movements, and the recovered power to dream beside her — but the gain is held to a modest level by the concluding « elle me manquait, je ne la possédais pas », which denies the possession the passage boasts of.
The reversal credits him with an unsuspected immense goodness that displaces the earlier verdict of atrocious malice, though the goodness is qualified by unfamiliar hardnesses.
The same reversal discovers depths of malice and perfidy in him, replacing the infinite delicacies he had been credited with, even though a frequent gentleness is allowed as compensation.

ambiguities: The evaluator behind E2 is Jupien's niece, an unnamed figure not on the reference sheet, so the appraisal is recorded with the narrator as reporting source; the narrator's framing sentence (« Ainsi n'avait-elle pas su porter un jugement plus défini … que moi sur Andrée … et sur Albertine ») explicitly withholds endorsement from her reversed verdicts.

The narrator's own standing in E1 is genuinely underdetermined in sign: the triumphal vocabulary of capture and theft is read here as ironized because of the cage imagery and the closing « je ne la possédais pas », but a reading that takes his pride at face value would make the same evidence a straightforward elevation.
